newsitem.title: HONG KONG: INTERVIEW-Asian refiners face slim profit margins.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Asian refiners face slim profit margins.

text.p: Asia's refinery profit margins have only slim prospects for improvement in the next few years because of a rise in refining capacity and slowing economic growth, Merrill Lynch said on Tuesday.

However, margins would improve from 1999 as Asia's demand outpaces supply more and more, James Brown, vice president of Securities Research and Economics at Merrill Lynch told Reuters in an interview.

"We've seen declining expectations of demand growth across the region, combined with commitments on the part of a number of the major oil companies in the early 1990s, which subsequently came onstream last year," he said.
"This has led to an environment of very sober refining margins...with little prospect for a near-term (12 month) sustained recovery," he said.

Simple oil refining margins slumped to an average $1.30 per barrel in 1996 in Singapore, a 1.2 million barrels-per-day (bpd) refining centre used as the bellweather for the state of the Asian industry. In the early 1990s they were three dollars per

Oil traders said Singapore refiners were currently suffering very shallow to negative margins and would launch a round of refinery run cuts in coming weeks if the situation did not improve. Esso Singapore, a unit of Exxon Corp, cut runs 10 percent, a source close to the company said on Tuesday.
Brown said the slide in margins was partly the result of Asia adding 1.2 million barrels-per-day (bpd) of refining capacity in 1996, relative to a base capacity of 18.1 million bpd.
South Korea added 620,000 bpd and Thailand added 275,000 bpd.
"This has flooded the South Korean market with middle distillates and the North Asian region is awash with middle distillates," Brown said.
He said the South Korean expansion was driven by competition over domestic market share, rather than financial returns.
"Bringing on 620,000 bpd near simultaneously is not a commercially prudent thing to do," he said.

"We've also seen volatility in refining margins, namely periodic bouts of product dumping, financial manipulation of prices and very strong seasonal fluctuation in demand, particularly around Chinese New Year," Brown said.
The analyst said he expected margins in 1997 to remain around $1.30, rising to $1.50 in 1998 and $1.70 in 1999 as the demand-supply of oil products turns in favour of regional refiners.
He said a number of factors were holding back development of refiners in the region, including financing problems, government regulatory hesitation and bureaucratic delays.

China has an unofficial policy of barring foreign investment in its refining sector, keeping refinery development for state-owned China Petrochemical Corp (Sinopec), which operates 80 percent of the country's refining capacity, Brown said.
"China is out of bounds," he said, adding this raised questions about China's efficiency in oil refining.
Asian governments were also hindered by a lack of cash needed to fund new refineries, an amount conservatively estimated by Brown at $70 billion over the next ten years to keep pace with demand.
